newsitem.title: UK: Fed fallout highlights chart dangers for T-bonds.
newsitem.headline: Fed fallout highlights chart dangers for T-bonds.

text.p: Everyone knew it was coming but there was only so much they could do to prevent the damage.
Tuesday's rise in U.S. interest rates has left both ends of the U.S. yield curve vulnerable and technical analysts on Wednesday predicted renewed weakness for Treasuries.
The main problem is not so much Tuesday's quarter percentage point tightening but the expectation of several more to come.
"You don't buy fixed income securities when the Fed starts a tightening cycle," said Bill Westgate, senior vice president at HSBC Securities in London.
"I don't know when the last tightening is going to be, but I'll tell you, this wasn't it," Westgate said.
He said a picture was forming of a global economic growth phase, which meant U.S. yields were clearly on the way up.
Tom Hobson, director of technical analysis at Merrill Lynch in London, said the chart signals from the interest rate futures market were alarming.
"The key to this market is the anticipation of future short-end rates," he said.
Benchmark September Eurodollars, after surging to 93.90 ahead of the Federal Reserve tightening, tumbled to a 93.78 finish on Tuesday.
The federal funds target rate was notched up to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent on Tuesday.
But Hobson said later-dated Eurodollar futures, as well as the spreads between 1997 and 1998 contracts, best showed the threats the Treasury market faced.

For instance, he said March 1998 Eurodollars were hovering just above important support at 93.39-40 on Tuesday. "If it breaks below that I think the short end market is going to have a lot of problems and Treasuries will follow."

He added that the spread between June 1997 and June 1998 Eurodollars had widened some 37 basis points since December, indicating the growing anxiety the market had about more drastic monetary policy tightening in the future.
At the long end, technical analysts said benchmark 30-year T-bond yields were showing signs of wanting to break higher.
Elizabeth Miller, technical analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said seven percent was more than a symbolic level for the long bond.

"It's not only psychological. It's the middle of a range through last year from April to October, so it's a pivot point," Miller said. She added that the market approached that level in late January and then again recently before Treasuries rallied.
Westgate of HSBC said the way large investors behaved at this juncture was critical.

"What we've seen in the last several weeks is the first wave of a bear market," he said, adding the big question was whether a more pernicious, second wave was on the way where large accounts decide to sell Treasuries rather than buy them around seven percent yields.
Miller said, "If we get through there (seven percent) we'll see 7.50 percent very quickly."

For the futures, the main threat was just below the 108-00 level. June T-bonds set a near six-month low at 107-31 on March 20. At 1045 GMT, they were at 108-24, little moved from late Tuesday but down from a 109-25 high earlier that day.
"Momentum is starting to look bearish," Miller said. Below 107-31, she said there was potential down to 106-06.

Chart watchers said that next major support area would be crucial for T-bonds. On continuation charts, T-bonds set three key lows on either side of 106-00 in June, July and September of last year. -- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6784
